name: Phytosphingosine

angle.text: Phytosphingosine is added to barrier-repair and blemish-prone skincare as a precursor to the skin's own ceramides, with the aim of reducing dryness and breakouts. Cosmetic trials of it were not found in the sources reviewed.

summary: A plant- and yeast-derived ceramide building block added to barrier and blemish skincare; cosmetic trials are not found in the sources reviewed.
note: Thin source base; claims rest on general ceramide biology.
currentQuick:
Phytosphingosine is a fatty-chain amino alcohol that cells use to build ceramides, lipids central to the skin barrier. It appears in some moisturisers and acne-prone skin products.
The sources reviewed contain no human studies of it as a cosmetic.
How it works: It is a precursor in sphingolipid and ceramide synthesis; the idea behind skincare use is to supply raw material for barrier lipids.
Risks and caveats: No cosmetic safety trials were found. The pure chemical carries eye-damage and environmental hazard classifications per Wikipedia.
deepLead:
Phytosphingosine is an 18-carbon sphingoid base (2-aminooctadecane-1,3,4-triol) abundant in plants and fungi and also present in animals. It is a building block of more complex sphingolipids, including certain ceramides.
In skincare it is added to products aimed at barrier support and blemish-prone skin, as a ceramide precursor. The sources reviewed contain little cosmetic-specific research on it, so claims about its skin effects rest largely on the general biology of sphingolipids and ceramides.
No human trial of topical phytosphingosine for appearance outcomes was found.

name: Cholesterol

angle.text: Cholesterol is included in ceramide-based moisturizers because it makes up roughly a third of the skin's barrier lipid mix, helping restore a dry or damaged barrier. It is used as part of lipid blends; appearance trials on its own were not found.

summary: The body's key membrane sterol and a third of the skin's barrier lipid mix; in skincare it shows up alongside ceramides, with no appearance trials on its own.
note: Blood cholesterol and topical cholesterol are different topics; heart-health guidance concerns the former.
currentQuick:
Cholesterol is a waxy lipid every animal cell uses. In skin it forms part of the lipid mortar, with ceramides and fatty acids, that holds water in.
Barrier-repair creams sometimes include it for that reason, but the sources reviewed contain no appearance trials of topical cholesterol.
How it works: In the stratum corneum it packs with ceramides and fatty acids into ordered layers that limit water loss. In the body it is a precursor to hormones, bile acids and vitamin D.
Risks and caveats: High blood LDL cholesterol is linked to heart disease and is treated under clinical guidelines. Topical cosmetic use was not assessed in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Cholesterol is the main sterol in animals: a structural component of cell membranes and a precursor to steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D. Nearly all animal cells can make it, with the liver and intestines producing about 80 percent of the daily total.
In skin, cholesterol is one of three main lipids in the stratum corneum, alongside ceramides and free fatty acids. Wikipedia describes this matrix as the 'mortar' that limits water loss, and gives a rough weight ratio of about 50 percent ceramides, 25 percent cholesterol and 15 percent free fatty acids. Barrier-repair moisturisers sometimes include cholesterol with ceramides for this reason.
In looksmaxxing discussion cholesterol also arises in diet and testosterone debates, where blood levels are weighed against cardiovascular risk. Clinical guidelines such as the NCEP Adult Treatment Panel III address blood cholesterol and heart disease.

name: Squalene

angle.text: Squalane and squalene are used as light, non-greasy emollients in moisturizers and facial oils to soften skin and add glow. Squalene is a natural component of skin sebum; trials for appearance outcomes are not found.

summary: A skin-identical oil used as a lightweight emollient; safe-looking but with no trials for appearance outcomes.
note: Also used in vaccine adjuvants; that research is unrelated to skin outcomes.
currentQuick:
Squalene is a natural oil that the body makes and that appears in skin sebum. In skincare it is used as a light emollient, sourced from shark liver, olive or amaranth oil, or made synthetically.
Its appearance benefits are described mostly in terms of its skin-like origin; no published human trial was found testing it for acne, ageing or texture.
How it works: It is an emollient that sits on and blends with the skin's lipid layer. In the body it is a step in making cholesterol.
Risks and caveats: Reviews summarised by Wikipedia report low toxicity and little allergy at cosmetic levels. Its many double bonds mean it can oxidise. Shark sourcing has been a conservation concern.
deepLead:
Squalene is an oily hydrocarbon (C30H50) and an intermediate in the biosynthesis of sterols such as cholesterol. It takes its name from Squalus, the shark genus whose liver oil was its first major source, and it is also made by the human body and secreted in skin sebum.
In personal care it is used as an emollient and lubricant in topical products. Sources include shark liver oil, olive oil and amaranth oil, plus synthetic and microbial production. Squalene is also an ingredient of oil-in-water emulsion adjuvants used in some vaccines.
Toxicology reviews summarised by Wikipedia indicate low acute toxicity and little contact allergy at cosmetic concentrations. The wiki found no published human trial testing squalene for an appearance outcome such as acne, wrinkles or skin texture.

name: Natto gum

angle.text: Natto gum is used in Japanese and Korean face packs and essences as a humectant that holds water on the skin, associated with poly-gamma-glutamic acid. Its use is documented in patents and product descriptions rather than human trials.

summary: A fermented-soybean polymer used as a humectant in face packs; documented in patents, not in trials.
note: Only patent-level sources were found.
currentQuick:
Natto gum is a sticky polymer from Bacillus fermentation of soybeans, listed in some face packs and moisturisers.
It appears in patents as a moisturising ingredient; no human study was found.
How it works: It is described as a water-binding, film-forming polymer that holds moisture on the skin, related to poly-gamma-glutamic acid.
Risks and caveats: No safety data were found in the sources reviewed. Soy-derived ingredients can be an allergen for some people.
deepLead:
Natto gum is a cosmetic ingredient described as a sticky, water-soluble polymer produced by Bacillus bacteria during fermentation of soybeans, as in the Japanese food natto. It is associated with poly-gamma-glutamic acid (gamma-PGA), a water-soluble biodegradable polymer made from glutamic acid.
Published sources on natto gum are mostly patents that list it as a moisturising or film-forming ingredient in face packs and creams. No human clinical studies of natto gum were located.

name: Lauric acid

angle.text: Lauric acid, abundant in coconut oil, is mostly a soap and cleanser raw material, and some users apply it with the idea of reducing acne bacteria for clearer skin. Antibacterial data come from lab studies; skin appearance trials are not found.

summary: A coconut-derived fatty acid that mostly serves as soap and surfactant raw material; lab antibacterial data, no skin trials.
note: Can irritate skin and eyes in concentrated form.
currentQuick:
Lauric acid is the main fatty acid in coconut oil and is used to make soaps and cleansing agents.
It is mentioned in acne talk because it inhibited some bacteria in laboratory tests; no skin trials were found.
How it works: It acts as a surfactant in cleansers, and in lab studies disrupts bacterial membranes.
Risks and caveats: Pure lauric acid can irritate skin and eyes. Dietary intake raises total and LDL cholesterol in trials.
deepLead:
Lauric acid (dodecanoic acid) is a saturated 12-carbon medium-chain fatty acid that makes up about half the fatty acids in coconut oil and palm kernel oil. It is used mainly to make soaps and surfactants for cosmetics and cleansers.
In skincare discussion it is cited for antimicrobial activity: a 1972 laboratory study of 30 fatty acids found lauric acid the most inhibitory saturated fatty acid against Gram-positive bacteria. The wiki found no clinical trial of lauric acid applied to skin for acne or other appearance outcomes.

name: Panthenol

angle.text: Panthenol is a staple of moisturizers, hair products and wound creams, used to hydrate skin, calm irritation and leave hair smoother. Human data mainly cover skin hydration and wound healing.

summary: Provitamin B5 humectant found in moisturisers and wound creams, with human data mainly for hydration and wound healing.
note: Hair-growth claims lack trial support in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Panthenol is a vitamin B5 derivative used in moisturisers, shampoos and healing ointments.
Studies and reviews describe hydration and post-procedure wound-healing roles; hair-growth claims are less supported.
How it works: Skin converts it to pantothenic acid, used to make coenzyme A, and it binds water as a humectant.
Risks and caveats: Usually well tolerated; rare contact dermatitis or allergy has been reported.
deepLead:
Panthenol is the alcohol analogue of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5). It is converted in the body to pantothenic acid, so it acts as a provitamin; dexpanthenol is the biologically active D form, while cosmetics may use D-panthenol or a racemic DL mixture.
It is used in moisturisers, hair products, lip care and wound-care ointments such as Bepanthen. Reviews describe moisturising and post-procedure wound-healing roles for dexpanthenol, and it is generally well tolerated, with rare contact allergy.

name: Jojoba oil

angle.text: Jojoba oil is used as a facial moisturizer and carrier oil because its wax esters resemble skin's own sebum, and is popular for softening skin and hair. It is widely used and valued by users; controlled trials on appearance are limited.

summary: A sebum-like liquid wax used as a moisturiser and carrier oil; popular, but with little trial data.
note: Not intended for ingestion.
currentQuick:
Jojoba oil is a golden liquid wax from a desert shrub, used in moisturisers and hair products.
Its sebum-like makeup is the main reason given for its use; trials specifically on appearance are scarce.
How it works: It forms a stable, occlusive layer on skin that reduces water loss, according to oil-comparison studies.
Risks and caveats: Rare contact dermatitis has been reported. It is not a food oil.
deepLead:
Jojoba oil is a liquid wax pressed from the seeds of Simmondsia chinensis, a shrub native to southern Arizona, southern California and northwestern Mexico. About 97 percent of it is long-chain wax esters rather than triglycerides, making it unusually stable.
It is common in moisturisers, shampoos and conditioners and is often described as resembling sebum. Reviews of plant oils discuss it among oils used for skin-barrier support, but the evidence is mostly small or laboratory studies.

name: Tamanu oil

angle.text: Tamanu oil is promoted in natural-skincare circles for fading scars and acne marks and calming breakouts, drawing on traditional Pacific use for wounds and burns. Support comes from lab cell data and tradition; human trials are not found.

summary: A Pacific nut oil promoted for scars and acne; lab cell data exist, human trials do not.
note: No clinical trial for scars or acne found.
currentQuick:
Tamanu oil comes from the nuts of a coastal tropical tree and has a long history in Pacific folk medicine.
It is sold for scars and acne. Lab studies on skin cells are encouraging in tone; human trials were not found.
How it works: In cell studies the oil raised skin-cell proliferation and collagen production; it also shows antioxidant activity.
Risks and caveats: Reported as low in toxicity at low concentrations; allergy data are limited.
deepLead:
Tamanu oil is a viscous green-yellow oil pressed from the nuts of Calophyllum inophyllum, a tropical tree of the Indo-Pacific. It has been used in traditional medicine in Polynesia, India and Southeast Asia for wounds, burns and skin conditions.
In skincare it is promoted for scars and acne. Laboratory work reports that a Polynesian tamanu oil emulsion stimulated proliferation and collagen production in cultured human skin cells, but the sources reviewed describe no completed clinical trial for scars or acne.

name: Meadowfoam seed oil

angle.text: Meadowfoam seed oil is used in creams, lip products and hair care as a light, very stable emollient that softens skin and adds shine. Its appeal is largely formulation stability; published human skin-benefit trials are not found.

summary: A very oxidation-stable plant oil from a Californian/Oregon wildflower, used as a cosmetic emollient with no published human skin-benefit trials.
note: Unrefined oil is not considered suitable for eating because of its erucic acid content.
currentQuick:
Meadowfoam seed oil is pressed from the seeds of Limnanthes alba, a small wildflower native to California and Oregon. It is used in cosmetic and hair-care products as an emollient, and is known for being unusually stable against oxidation.
Published work on it is mostly about formulation and chemistry. One 2021 cosmetic-science study tested it as a pigment-dispersing agent in lipstick. No published human trials were found on its effects on skin appearance.
How it works: Its fatty acids are mostly very long-chain (C20 and C22) types such as eicosenoic and docosadienoic acid, which the sources link to its resistance to going rancid. In products it acts as an emollient and a dispersing agent for pigments.
Risks and caveats: Reference sources note that unpurified meadowfoam oil is not suitable for human consumption because of high erucic acid. Topical safety data from clinical studies were not found. The plant's commercial crops have been vulnerable to fungal disease.
deepLead:
Meadowfoam seed oil is a vegetable oil obtained from the seeds of Limnanthes alba (white meadowfoam), an annual herb in the family Limnanthaceae native to wet grasslands, vernal pools and moist woodland in California and Oregon. The seeds contain roughly 20 to 30 percent oil, which is made up of more than 98 percent long-chain fatty acids.
In cosmetics and hair care the oil is used for its emollient quality, soft skin feel and stability. Published research on it is largely technical: a 2021 study in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science evaluated it as a natural pigment-dispersing agent in lipstick, compared with castor oil and octyldodecanol. No clinical studies of its effect on human skin or appearance were found.

name: Sea buckthorn oil

angle.text: Sea buckthorn oil is used in creams and supplements for its orange carotenoid-rich profile, promoted for moisturizing, glow and skin repair. Small human trials exist, but skin-specific appearance evidence is limited.

summary: A carotenoid-rich orange oil from Hippophae berries and seeds, used in creams and supplements, with small human trials but little skin-specific evidence.
note: Studies on skin aging exist as registrations but published human skin results were not found among the sources.
currentQuick:
Sea buckthorn oil is taken from the berry pulp and seeds of Hippophae rhamnoides, a hardy shrub of Europe and Asia. The pulp oil is orange to deep red, rich in carotenoids and palmitoleic acid, while the seed oil is richer in linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid.
It is added to creams, lotions and supplements and is promoted for skin repair and anti-aging. Published human studies cover dry eye and other mucosal conditions; a skin-aging trial was registered, but no published human skin results were found.
How it works: Proponents attribute its effects to carotenoids, vitamin E, sterols and unsaturated fatty acids with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Laboratory work on human skin cells found that seed oil altered lipid metabolism changes induced by UV exposure.
Risks and caveats: Reviews describe the oil as generally well tolerated in the trials cited, but safety data specific to cosmetic use are limited. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and food supplement; regulatory status varies by country.
deepLead:
Sea buckthorn oil is a golden-orange to red oil obtained from the berries, seeds and sometimes leaves of the shrub Hippophae rhamnoides (now also classed as Elaeagnus rhamnoides), native to temperate Europe and Asia. Pulp oil and seed oil differ in composition: pulp oil is rich in palmitoleic acid and carotenoids, whereas seed oil is richer in linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids.
The oil is used in creams, lotions, hair products and dietary supplements, and is marketed for skin repair, hydration and anti-aging. Human trials of the oil have mostly examined oral use for dry eye and mucosal dryness; one trial of oral and topical use on skin aging was registered in 2008. Reviews describe much of the other evidence as preclinical.

name: Evening primrose oil

chain: Support for skin barrier and inflammation
angle.text: Evening primrose oil is taken as a supplement or applied topically for dry, eczema-prone or hormonally breakout-prone skin. Reviews of its use for eczema find insufficient evidence, and appearance trials in healthy skin are not found.

summary: A gamma-linolenic acid-rich seed oil sold as a supplement and skin product; reviews find insufficient evidence for eczema or other conditions.
note: May increase bleeding risk; caution advised in pregnancy and seizure disorders.
currentQuick:
Evening primrose oil is pressed from the seeds of Oenothera biennis, a North American plant. It contains linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) and is sold mainly as an oral dietary supplement, also appearing in skin-care products.
It has been studied for atopic eczema, breast pain, menopausal symptoms and other conditions. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, as summarised in reference sources, describes the evidence as insufficient for any medical condition, and a Cochrane review found no effect on eczema.
How it works: GLA is an omega-6 fatty acid that the body converts to prostaglandin precursors; proponents argue this supports skin barrier and inflammatory balance. The proposed link to appearance outcomes has mostly been tested in eczema rather than cosmetic skin quality.
Risks and caveats: Described as likely safe at recommended amounts, with headache and nausea reported. It may raise bleeding risk, and sources advise caution in people with seizure disorders or mania and in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Herb-drug interaction reviews list it among herbal products of interest.
deepLead:
Evening primrose oil (EPO) is a vegetable oil obtained from the seeds of the common evening primrose, Oenothera biennis, a North American plant that became naturalised across much of the world. The seeds contain about 24 percent oil, rich in the polyunsaturated fatty acids linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA).
Its main commercial use is as an oral dietary supplement, and it is also used in some skin products. It has been examined in trials for atopic eczema, breast pain, menopausal symptoms and other conditions. A Cochrane review reported in reference sources found no effect on eczema, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) is cited as finding the evidence insufficient to support use for any medical condition.

name: Macadamia oil

angle.text: Macadamia oil is used in moisturizers, body oils and hair products as a rich emollient, with interest in its palmitoleic acid, which is also found in skin sebum. Composition research exists; clear human skin-appearance trials are not found.

summary: A palmitoleic- and oleic-rich nut oil used as a cosmetic emollient and cooking oil, with composition research but no clear human skin-appearance trials.
note: Nut allergy is a consideration for any macadamia-derived product.
currentQuick:
Macadamia oil is pressed from the kernels of Macadamia integrifolia and related trees native to eastern Australia. It is mostly monounsaturated, with oleic acid and an unusual amount of palmitoleic acid, and it is used both in cooking and as an emollient in skin and hair products.
Research in the sources covers its fatty acids, oxidative stability and effects of dietary palmitoleic acid on blood lipids. No published human trial was found testing it on skin appearance.
How it works: As a topical ingredient it works as an emollient and fragrance fixative. Its low polyunsaturated content is linked to good oxidative stability. Palmitoleic acid has been studied in diet and metabolism research, not in skin-care trials.
Risks and caveats: Sources do not describe specific topical safety data. As a tree-nut product it can matter to people with nut allergy, a general consideration rather than a finding in the supplied studies.
deepLead:
Macadamia oil is a non-volatile oil pressed from the kernels of the macadamia tree, chiefly Macadamia integrifolia, a species native to Australia and now grown commercially. It is mostly monounsaturated: oleic acid is the main fatty acid, and palmitoleic acid, unusual in plant oils, is also present in notable amounts.
It is used as a frying and salad oil and in cosmetics, where it serves as an emollient and fragrance fixative. Research involving it covers composition across cultivars and oxidative stability; studies of palmitoleic acid look at blood lipids and metabolism rather than skin. No clinical studies of its effect on human appearance were found.

name: Grapeseed oil

angle.text: Grapeseed oil is used as a lightweight facial and massage oil, often chosen by people with oily or breakout-prone skin who want moisture without heaviness. Its linoleic acid content is documented; published trials on skin appearance are not found.

summary: A linoleic-rich by-product of winemaking used as a light cosmetic and cooking oil, with no published trials on skin appearance.
note: Some batches have been found to contain polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons from seed drying.
currentQuick:
Grapeseed oil is pressed from the seeds left over from winemaking. It is mostly linoleic acid (omega-6), light in texture, and used in cooking, massage oils, cosmetics and hair-care products.
Reference sources say it contains negligible polyphenols, unlike the seeds themselves, and that clinical research has been too weak to show any reduction in disease risk. No clinical trials on skin appearance were found.
How it works: Linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid found in skin lipids, and topical linoleic-rich oils are a common emollient choice. The sources do not report mechanistic studies of grapeseed oil on skin. Studies compare its oxidative stability with other edible oils.
Risks and caveats: Reference sources note that the oil has occasionally been found to contain dangerous levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, likely from combustion gases during seed drying, and a 2000 study examined how processing affects this content. Its high polyunsaturated content makes it prone to oxidation.
deepLead:
Grapeseed oil is a vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of grapes, a by-product of winemaking, with production concentrated in wine regions such as the Mediterranean. It is mostly linoleic acid (about 70 percent by one estimate) followed by oleic acid, with small amounts of vitamin E and plant sterols.
It is used as a light salad and cooking oil, a massage oil, and in some cosmetics and hair-care products, though the cosmetic claim is uncited in the reference source. Reference sources state that, unlike the seeds, the oil contains negligible polyphenols, and that as of 2016 clinical research was too weak to show disease-risk reduction. No clinical studies on skin or hair appearance were found.

name: Black rice extract

angle.text: Black rice extract is promoted in anti-aging and brightening skincare for its anthocyanin pigments, which act as antioxidants. Lab and animal work is plentiful; human skin evidence was not found.

summary: An anthocyanin-rich antioxidant extract from pigmented rice; lab and animal work is plentiful, but human skin evidence was not found.
note: Most research is in cells, animals or food science; small human trials are registered on other outcomes.
currentQuick:
Black rice extract is a pigment-rich preparation from the bran of dark-coloured Oryza sativa rice, concentrated in anthocyanins. It is marketed in supplements and some skin-care products as an antioxidant botanical.
Published work includes cell, mouse and fruit-fly experiments and food-science studies. Human trials exist as registrations on metabolic, cognitive and immune outcomes; none testing skin appearance were found.
How it works: Anthocyanins are plant pigments with antioxidant activity. Laboratory studies report that black rice extract raised antioxidant enzyme activity (superoxide dismutase and catalase) in cells and mice and reduced inflammatory signalling in macrophage cells.
Risks and caveats: No safety signals are described in the sources, and rice-based foods are widely eaten. Extract-specific safety data from human trials were not found. Anthocyanin stability and bioavailability are active research topics.
deepLead:
Black rice extract is a pigment-rich preparation obtained from the bran of dark-pigmented rice (Oryza sativa), whose colour comes mainly from anthocyanins. The grain is also called purple or forbidden rice; reference sources describe the "forbidden" label as a marketing term tied to claims of royal-only consumption.
The extract is studied and sold as an antioxidant botanical. Laboratory work reports antioxidant enzyme induction and reduced inflammatory signalling in cells, and mouse studies report effects on liver fat and, in fruit flies, lifespan. Small human trials have been registered on metabolism, cognition, immunity and stress, but no published trial on skin or appearance was found.

name: Propolis

angle.text: Propolis is a K-beauty staple in ampoules and creams, used for calming breakouts, soothing skin and giving a glowy finish. Antimicrobial data come from lab studies; skin-specific human evidence is limited.

summary: Bee-resin K-beauty extract with lab antimicrobial data, little skin-specific human evidence and a known contact-allergy risk.
note: Recognised cause of allergic contact dermatitis, especially in people sensitive to bee products.
currentQuick:
Propolis is the resin bees collect and blend with wax to seal their hives. Skincare brands use extracts of it for soothing and clarifying claims, drawing on its long folk-medicine history.
Research is mostly laboratory-based or in other fields such as dental and metabolic health. Published human trials on cosmetic skin outcomes were not found among the sources reviewed.
How it works: Laboratory studies attribute antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity to its flavonoids and phenolics, including CAPE, which inhibits NF-kappa B signalling in cell experiments. Composition varies widely by origin.
Risks and caveats: Contact allergy is the main documented risk, with skin inflammation and lip swelling reported from topical products. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and supplement; no special approval for skin benefits is reported.
deepLead:
Propolis, also called bee glue, is a sticky resinous mixture that honey bees make from plant exudates such as tree-bud resins and sap, combined with beeswax and saliva. Bees use it to seal gaps in the hive and to coat its interior surfaces . Its composition varies with the hive's location, season and local plants, and it typically includes flavonoids, phenolic acids and terpenoids .
In skincare, propolis appears as an extract in K-beauty and natural-cosmetic products, where brands market it for soothing, blemish-prone and dull-looking skin. Proponents point to its long traditional use and to laboratory findings of antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity .
Published evidence for cosmetic skin benefits in humans is limited. Most of the literature consists of laboratory and review work on propolis constituents, and clinical trials registered for propolis concern other uses such as oral health and general medicine. Propolis is also a recognised cause of allergic contact dermatitis .

name: Honey (topical)

angle.text: Honey is used in DIY masks and skincare as a humectant for soft, hydrated skin, and some users apply it for brightening and blemishes. It has real wound-care data; controlled evidence for skin brightening is not yet available.

summary: A moisture-drawing pantry staple with real wound-care data but no controlled evidence yet for skin brightening.
note: Evidence is from wound care; cosmetic brightening is untested. Not for infants under one.
currentQuick:
Honey is used on skin as a mask or ingredient for hydration and a softer, brighter look. It has a long folk history on burns and wounds.
Trials exist for wounds, mouth ulcers and eye conditions, but none found address cosmetic brightening.
How it works: Honey is hygroscopic, so it attracts and holds water at the skin surface. Its antibacterial properties are attributed to compounds such as methylglyoxal and hydrogen peroxide, under preliminary study.
Risks and caveats: Generally well tolerated as a food. Infant botulism is the best-documented risk of honey, and allergy is possible in sensitive people.
deepLead:
Topical honey refers to honey applied to the skin, either as a home remedy and mask ingredient or as a processed ingredient in skincare. Honey is hygroscopic, meaning it draws in moisture, which is the basis for its use as a humectant . It also has a long folk use on burns and skin injuries .
In appearance skincare, honey is promoted for hydration, softening and a 'brightening' or clarifying effect. Clinical research on honey has focused mainly on wound care and mucosal conditions rather than on cosmetic skin outcomes.
Wikipedia reports that medical-grade honey products have been approved by the FDA for minor wounds and burns, while evidence for many other uses is low quality .

name: Bee venom (topical)

angle.text: Topical bee venom is marketed in Korean skincare as a natural alternative to botulinum toxin, with brands claiming it tightens skin and smooths expression lines. Wrinkle trials of the topical product were not found.

summary: Korean 'faux-tox' bee-venom cream with no wrinkle trials found and an allergen-heavy ingredient.
note: Venom contains a major bee-sting allergen; wrinkle claims are untested.
currentQuick:
Bee venom creams are marketed as a gentler stand-in for Botox-style injections. Brands say they tighten and smooth lines.
The only controlled human trial identified tested an ointment on jaw muscle tension, not wrinkles.
How it works: Venom contains melittin and enzymes that are bioactive in lab settings. How a cream would deliver them through skin to relax facial muscle is not shown in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Phospholipase A2 is a main allergen, and venom can cause local inflammation. Data on cosmetic-product safety were not found.
deepLead:
Topical bee venom is honey bee venom, or a purified or synthetic version of it, used in creams and masks marketed in Korean skincare as a natural 'faux-tox' alternative to botulinum toxin injections for wrinkles. Brand claims generally describe it as tightening or smoothing expression lines.
Honey bee venom is a mixture of peptides and enzymes. Melittin makes up roughly half of the venom peptides, phospholipase A2 is a main allergen, and apamin, hyaluronidase and histamine are also present .
Published human evidence for wrinkle reduction was not found among the sources reviewed. The one identified controlled human study of bee venom ointment concerned jaw-muscle tension, not appearance .

name: Galactomyces ferment filtrate

chain: Yeast ferment of vitamins and amino acids
angle.text: Galactomyces ferment filtrate, sold in Japanese and Korean essences such as Pitera, is used for brightening, hydration and a smoother glow. Evidence includes cell-lab data and product studies; isolated human trials are few.

summary: Sake-yeast ferment behind brightening essences, with cell-lab data and product studies but few isolated human trials.
note: Human studies test multi-ingredient products, so GFF-specific effects are unclear.
currentQuick:
GFF is a filtrate from yeast-fermented sake used in essences for hydration, texture and glow. Its story starts with sake brewers' youthful hands.
Product studies report improvements in pores, roughness and pigmentation, but they involve formulas with other ingredients.
How it works: Cell studies report changes in keratinocyte differentiation, barrier-related proteins and inflammatory signalling. The exact active compounds are unidentified.
Risks and caveats: Patch tests are reported as non-irritating in secondary sources. No serious safety signals were found in the sources reviewed, though long-term data are limited.
deepLead:
Galactomyces ferment filtrate (GFF) is a cosmetic ingredient obtained from the fermentation of sake using Galactomyces yeast strains. It is marketed under trade names such as Pitera and is used in brightening and hydrating essences, especially in Japanese and Korean skincare .
Its use is traced to the observation that the hands of sake brewers, who work with yeast fermentation, stayed youthful-looking, a story repeated in the scientific literature on the ingredient . Products based on GFF are sold widely around the world .
Most research is laboratory work on skin cells plus several cosmetic studies of GFF-containing products on volunteers, including a multi-year longitudinal study. Those product studies test formulations that contain other ingredients, so effects cannot be attributed to GFF alone, and independent controlled trials of GFF in isolation were not found among the sources reviewed.

name: Bifida ferment lysate

angle.text: Bifida ferment lysate is used in repair and barrier serums as a probiotic-derived active, promoted for soothing, resilience and a more youthful look. Lab barrier data exist; human trials are limited to combination products.

summary: Probiotic-derived ferment in repair serums, with lab barrier data and only combination-product trials.
note: Human studies used multi-ingredient products, so BFL's own effect is unclear.
currentQuick:
BFL comes from fermented, broken-down Bifidobacterium and is added to serums for barrier repair and soothing.
Lab studies are positive in cell models, while human studies tested combination products.
How it works: A 2023 cell study reported strengthened barrier function and stable skin defense signalling. How this translates to human skin is not established.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms were found in the reviewed sources. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, and prolonged sheet-mask wear has been linked to skin irritation generally.
deepLead:
Bifida ferment lysate (BFL) is a cosmetic ingredient obtained by fermenting Bifidobacterium and then breaking down (lysing) the cells and extracting the result. It is used in repair and barrier serums as a 'probiotic' or postbiotic active .
Researchers describe semi-active or inactive probiotics and their extracts as having properties that may soothe irritated skin and support the skin barrier, and Bifidobacterium has been studied for acne and atopic dermatitis . Under the 2021 ISAPP definition, a postbiotic is a preparation of inanimate microorganisms or their components that confers a health benefit; Wikipedia notes postbiotic research is emerging and needs confirmation in well-designed human studies .
Evidence specific to BFL for appearance outcomes consists of laboratory work and a few clinical studies of multi-ingredient products.

Lactobacillus ferment is a bacterial-ferment ingredient used in 'probiotic' creams for calming and barrier support.
Human evidence is sparse: a scalp-microbiome study of a combined ferment is the closest found.
How it works: Postbiotic ingredients are proposed to influence skin microbiome and barrier signalling, but mechanisms for this specific ferment were not shown in the sources reviewed.

deepLead:
Lactobacillus ferment (often listed on labels as Lactobacillus ferment or ferment lysate) is a cosmetic ingredient made by fermenting with Lactobacillus bacteria. It is used in K-beauty and 'probiotic skincare' products for barrier-support and soothing claims.
In the broader category, the ISAPP definition describes a postbiotic as a preparation of inanimate microorganisms or their components that confers a health benefit; Wikipedia describes postbiotic research as emerging and in need of confirmation in well-designed human studies .
Evidence for appearance outcomes is thin. The sources reviewed include a scalp-microbiome study of a combined Saccharomyces and Lactobacillus ferment and a rat study of a Lactobacillus-fermented food supplement for blood lipids, not facial-skin trials.
